newsitem.title: USA: Designers putting best foot forward.
newsitem.headline: Designers putting best foot forward.

text.p: Looking to offer a complete head-to-toe look, popular designer brands such as Nautica, Tommy Hilfiger and Ralph Lauren have signed licensing deals with footwear companies to offer a fashionable alternative to sneakers.

"Because of the size and scope of the overall athletic market, there's no question the biggest opportunity for any of the designers is the athletic footwear market," said Jim Boscamp, president of Nautica Footwear.

Nautica Footwear, a unit of Genesco Inc., signed Charlotte Hornets forward Glen Rice, the 1997 basketball All-Star Game Most Valuable Player, to a three-year contract earlier this year to add authenticity to its sports line, Boscamp said.
Rice's Nautica Competition shoe will be in retail stores, where Nautica and the other fashion designers have taken hold, and in speciality athletic footwear stores in August.
Nautica is the only one of the designer brands to sign a major sports star to a marketing contract.

Rather than directly attack the authentic sports shoe market, other designers plan to capitalize on their fashion appeal and offer a variety of styles, including athletic, athletic leisure, casual and dress casual.
The designer brands are just beginning to step into the footwear arena, but are expected to grow quickly and go toe-to-toe with other athletic footwear companies, analysts said.

Brett Barakett, an analyst with Salomon Brothers, said he expected the designer brands to account for about 7 percent, or nearly $600 million, of the estimated $8.5 billion U.S. athletic footwear market by 1999.
For the designers, an entry into athletic footwear gives them a chance to leverage their strong brand names and extend their product offerings to a high-margin business.
"The athletic footwear market has been growing at a phenomenal rate over the past five or six years," Barakett said. "The margins in athletic footwear are phenomenal, much stronger than apparel."

He believes the strongest players in the designer category will be Polo Ralph Lauren Corp., which has paired with Reebok International Ltd.'s Rockport Co.; Tommy Hilfiger and its partner Stride Rite Corp.; and Nautica Enterprises Inc. and Genesco.

"Obviously, a brand name like Polo is one of the top names in the world," said Rockport President Angel Martinez. "It gives us a growth opportunity with Ralph Lauren and Polo Sport that we just wouldn't have with Rockport."
An athletic line under the Polo Sport name will be launched next spring and men's and women's casual dress shoes under the Ralph Lauren name will be out in this fall.

Polo Sport and Ralph Lauren will be able to tap Rockport's expertise in design, sourcing and distribution, and will probably be the most successful of the designer brands, Barakett said. He expects sales from the licensing deal to top $180 million by 1999.
Stride Rite Chief Executive Robert Siegel said he expects sales of more than $40 million this year from its licensing deal with Tommy Hilfiger.
The Hilfiger deal gives Stride Rite, primarily a women's and children's brand, a strong foothold in the men's and athletic footwear category, Siegel said.

A high-top basketball shoe named "The Fly," which sports a zippered top and retails for about $100, immediately sold out upon its introduction this spring and has been an unexpected success for the Hilfiger line.

"When we originally signed the deal with Tommy Hilfiger, we knew there would be a big opportunity on the casual side. What we really didn't anticipate was that the athletic portion would be as big as it is," Siegel said.
Not all sneaker companies have elected to join the fashion footwear parade.
Most noticeably absent is Nike Inc.

"Fashion - it's jokingly referred to as the f-word here," said Jim Small, manager of public relations with Nike. "If we were going to throw in the fashion component, we would alienate the core consumer, who is an athlete. They are going to see us an inauthentic."
Barakett said Nike, which will spend an estimated $800 million in marketing alone in 1997, has little to lose to the designer brands.
"No kid is going to buy a Tommy Hilfiger and go play hoops in them," he said. "I don't think we'll be seeing a Donna Karan shoe running in the New York Marathon."
